citations.F1: `serialize_event` does one `SELECT ... FROM users` per row, sequentially awaited — that's 1,900+ round trips (N+1); batch with one `SELECT id, display_name, avatar_url FROM users WHERE id = ANY($1)`
citations.F2: `seen: list[str]` + `if ev["dedupe_key"] in seen` is O(n²) dedupe over up to thousands of rows; make `seen` a `set`.
citations.F3: `lookup_geo` makes a **synchronous** `requests.get` call inside an async endpoint — this blocks the entire event loop for that worker
citations.F4: no index on (org_id, created_at) — the query does a full scan/sort of 4.2M rows every call; add `CREATE INDEX events_org_id_created_at_idx ON events (org_id, created_at DESC)`
citations.F5: `_request_timings: list[float]` also grows unbounded for the life of the process — same leak pattern, feeds into the same OOM; cap it (ring buffer)
citations.F6: `_geo_cache: dict[str, dict]` is a module-level dict with no eviction — it grows one entry per unique IP forever ... Bound it (LRU/TTL cache)
citations.F9: bumping to 16/50 now would mainly let more blocked-event-loop requests pile up concurrently, hiding the real bug and increasing DB connection pressure (6 pods × 16 workers × 50 = 4800 potential connections). ... Response caching (Redis, 60s) is reasonable as a later optimization for hot orgs, not as the fix
